question: What model architecture do the authors propose?
ground_truth: The Transformer, a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
answer:
The authors propose the Transformer, a model architecture that relies entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output, eschewing sequence-aligned recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or convolutions entirely (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 2).

Key features of the architecture include:

Encoder-Decoder Structure: Both the encoder and decoder are built using stacked self-attention and point-wise fully connected layers (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3).
Encoder: Composed of a stack of $N = 6$ identical layers, each featuring a multi-head self-attention mechanism followed by a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3).
Decoder: Also composed of a stack of $N = 6$ identical layers, with an additional sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the encoder's output, alongside masked multi-head self-attention to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3, 5).
Attention Mechanism: Utilizes "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" and "Multi-Head Attention," which allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4–5).
Positional Encoding: Because the model contains no recurrence or convolution, positional encodings are added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks to give the model information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).

question: What is the formula for scaled dot-product attention?
ground_truth: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
answer:
The formula for scaled dot-product attention is:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Where:

$Q$ is the matrix of queries (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$K$ is the matrix of keys (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$V$ is the matrix of values (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$d_k$ is the dimension of the keys, used as a scaling factor ($\sqrt{d_k}$) to prevent the softmax function from having extremely small gradients for large values of $d_k$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

question: Why are the dot products scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k)?
ground_truth: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling counteracts this.
answer:
The dot products are scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ to prevent them from growing too large in magnitude when the key dimension ($d_k$) is large (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

Here is why that matters:

Variance growth: If the components of the query ($q$) and key ($k$) are independent random variables with a mean of 0 and variance of 1, their dot product has a mean of 0 and a variance of $d_k$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4). As $d_k$ increases, the dot products grow much larger in magnitude.
Gradient vanishing: Large dot products are passed into the softmax function, pushing it into regions with extremely small gradients (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4). This slows down or halts effective training.

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ scales the variance back down to 1, keeping the softmax function in a healthy gradient range 📉 (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

question: What are the three ways multi-head attention is used in the Transformer?
ground_truth: Encoder-decoder attention (queries from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder output), encoder self-attention, and decoder self-attention (masked to prevent leftward information flow).
answer:
The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three distinct ways (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 5):

Encoder-decoder attention layers: The queries come from the previous decoder layer, while the keys and values come from the output of the encoder. This allows every position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the input sequence.
Encoder self-attention layers: In the encoder's self-attention layer, the queries, keys, and values all come from the output of the previous layer in the encoder, allowing every position to attend to all positions in the previous encoder layer.
Decoder self-attention layers: Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow every position to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. Masking is used to prevent leftward information flow and preserve the auto-regressive property.

question: Why are the dot products scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k)?
ground_truth: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling counteracts this.

The dot products are scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ primarily to prevent the gradients from becoming extremely small during training. 📉

Large Magnitudes: As the dimension of the keys ($d_k$) increases, the magnitude of the dot products tends to grow.
Softmax Saturation: When these dot products are very large, the softmax function is pushed into regions where its gradient is extremely small (it "saturates"). This makes it very difficult for the model to learn effectively through backpropagation.
Statistical Normalization: If you assume the components of the query and key are independent random variables with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, their dot product will have a mean of 0 but a variance of $d_k$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ scales the variance back down to 1, keeping the values in a range where the softmax function remains sensitive to changes.

(b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4)

question: Why did the authors choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
ground_truth: Results were nearly identical, and the sinusoidal version may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training.
answer:
The authors of the "Attention Is All You Need" paper chose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones for two primary reasons:

Relative Position Learning: They hypothesized that the sinusoidal functions would make it easier for the model to learn to attend to relative positions. This is because, for any fixed offset $k$, the encoding at position $pos+k$ can be represented as a linear function of the encoding at position $pos$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).
Length Extrapolation: The authors believed that using a fixed sinusoidal function might allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).

While they also experimented with learned positional embeddings and found the results to be nearly identical, they ultimately opted for the sinusoidal version due to these potential advantages 🧠.
